name: Romania
summary: Formed by uniting Wallachia and Moldavia in 1859, independent in 1878, enlarged in 1918, a communist state under Ceaușescu, and a democracy since 1989.

knownFor.label: Dracula legend
knownFor.note: Linked to the prince Vlad III.

terrain.value: Carpathian Mountains, Transylvanian plateau, Danube plain.

climate.value: Continental, with cold winters and hot summers.

resources.value: Fertile farmland, oil and gas (Ploiești was a major oilfield), timber and salt.

disasters.value: Earthquakes (Vrancea, 1977, about 1,500 dead) and Danube floods.

urbanisation.value: About 54% urban; Bucharest has about 2 million people, followed by Cluj-Napoca, Iași and Timișoara.

disease.value: Life expectancy around 76 years; the health service is underfunded and many doctors have emigrated.

migration.value: Several million Romanians work abroad, especially in Italy, Spain and Germany.

economicBase.value: Cars (Dacia), IT services, farming, energy and manufacturing.

tradeRoutes.value: The Danube and the Black Sea port of Constanța; in the EU single market since 2007.

moneyAndTax.value: The Romanian leu; a low 10% flat income tax.

inequality.value: Large gaps between cities and poor rural areas; Roma communities face discrimination and poverty.

governmentType.value: A semi-presidential republic: an elected president and a prime minister responsible to parliament.

keyRulers.value: Carol I (first king). Nicolae Ceaușescu (communist leader, 1965–89).

succession.value: Monarchy until 1947; communist party rule 1947–89; elections since 1990.

institutions.value: Parliament, a Constitutional Court and a National Anti-Corruption Directorate.

stability.value: The 1989 revolution began in December 1989 in Timișoara.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the Social Democrats, Liberals and new nationalist parties.

armyAndTech.value: NATO member since 2004; hosts allied troops and missile defence.

majorWars.value: Independence War (1877–78); both world wars, changing sides in 1944.

territoryChange.value: “Greater Romania” after 1918 added Transylvania and Bessarabia; lost Bessarabia to the USSR in 1940.

alliancesRivals.value: Joined NATO on 29 March 2004 and the EU on 1 January 2007.

scienceEducation.value: Universities in Bucharest, Cluj and Iași; strong in mathematics and IT.

communicationTransport.value: Rail network, growing motorways and the Danube.

religion.value: About 85% Romanian Orthodox; Catholic and Protestant minorities in Transylvania.

languageWriting.value: Romanian, a Romance language descended from Latin; Hungarian is spoken by a large minority.

artsArchitecture.value: Painted monasteries of Bukovina, Transylvanian fortified churches, the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși.

socialStructure.value: Romanian majority; Hungarian (about 6%) and Roma minorities.

sharedIdentity.value: Latin roots, Orthodox faith and the union of 1918.

dailyLife.value: Village houses and apartment blocks; sarmale, mămăligă.

ideasReligions.value: Strong links with Moldova, which shares its language.

colonisation.value: Wallachia and Moldavia were under Ottoman overlordship for centuries; Transylvania was ruled by Hungary and Austria.

riseSignals.value: Moldavia and Wallachia united in 1859 under Alexandru Ioan Cuza.

peakPeriod.value: Interwar “Greater Romania” (1918–40) and fast growth after EU entry (2007).

declineSignals.value: Hardship and repression under Ceaușescu in the 1980s.

outcome.value: Independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1877; the Great Union of 1 December 1918.
